title: HanoiWaterWatch
html:
HanoiWaterWatch

A live sensor network on Hanoi’s drain outfalls. Every discharge, seen within minutes.

Low-cost solar stations measure the outflow every two seconds and warn the city and nearby residents the moment untreated wastewater enters the river.

Read the summaryTry the live demo
  • 3stations in the pilot
  • 2 sbetween readings
  • 3bad readings to alert
  • Labcheck before a fine

Our design questionHow might we detect untreated wastewater discharges into Hanoi’s rivers in real time?

Problem
Discharges are found days late, and the polluter cannot be traced.
Solution
Sensor stations at outfalls, a colour-coded map app and instant alerts.
Who benefits
Riverside residents, environment authorities, downstream farmers.
Pilot cost
₫41,799,438 in Q190 core equipment for three stations, or ₫43,482,944 with one optional shared pH kit. The three-year planning budget is ₫339,314,885 including 20% contingency and internal allowances; it is not a supplier quotation.
Status
Working simulated prototype; user testing in progress.

Why it matters

The cost of finding out too late

Treatment30%

of Hanoi’s daily domestic wastewater, about one million m³, is treated.

VnExpress (2024)
Economy3.5%

of Vietnam’s GDP could be lost each year by 2035 through water pollution.

Viet Nam News (2019), citing the World Bank
Budget₫75,115 bn

approved in 2026 to restore one river, the Nhuệ.

Văn Anh (2026)
Downstream10–15

waves of Hanoi wastewater reach Hà Nam each year, killing farmed fish.

Báo Pháp Luật (2021)

Background

Rivers as open drains

The Tô Lịch, Kim Ngưu and Nhuệ rivers carry the wastewater of a fast-growing city, from both homes and industry (Nguyen et al., 2018).

Factory discharges are linked to high organic pollution in the Tô Lịch (Nguyen, 2019). In 2024, wastewater from the Thanh Oai Industrial Cluster failed national standards and residents reported skin irritation (Dai Doan Ket, 2024).

13 of 15

heavily polluted monitoring points lie in the Nhuệ–Đáy basin.

Báo Pháp Luật (2021)
Zn, Cr

Metals in the sediments of four urban rivers pose a considerable ecological risk.

Phung et al. (2024)

Problem

Four causes, four matching harms

Hover or tap a pair to follow the chain.

Residents and farmers near Hanoi’s drain outfalls need to know within minutes when untreated wastewater enters the water they use, because discharges happen when nobody is watching and are confirmed only days later.

Cause

Consequence

Testing is periodic and slowSamples are taken from time to time and lab results take days.
Pollution is found too lateIt has already harmed fish, crops and people.
Treatment is missing in clustersThe city only set a target for every operating cluster to treat wastewater in 2025 (Nguyet, 2025).
Metals build up in riversZinc and chromium accumulate in sediments (Phung et al., 2024).
Water data is rarely publicResidents cannot see when nearby water is unsafe.
People use contaminated waterResidents near Thanh Oai reported skin irritation (Dai Doan Ket, 2024).
Homes and factories share drainsMixed flows make polluters hard to identify.
The public paysClean-up costs fall on the city budget and farmers, not polluters.

title: Design
html:
Home / Design

Design

Six criteria drawn from stakeholder needs, three different options, and one weighted decision.

Design criteriaSolution optionsDesign selection

Design criteria

What a good solution must do

Each criterion comes from a stakeholder need in the Background. The ring shows its weight in the decision.

25%

Timely

Detects a limit breach and alerts within minutes, day or night.

Why: Discharges happen at night; lab tests take five days.

20%

Traceable

Links every reading to one outfall, a time and a calibration record; a lab sample confirms before any fine.

Why: Authorities need evidence that holds up.

20%

Reliable

Keeps false alarms rare and flags faulty or missing readings.

Why: Residents ignore alerts that are often wrong.

15%

Clear for residents

Vietnamese language, colour paired with text and symbols, readable by older users.

Why: The people most affected are often the least digital.

10%

Durable

Survives dirty water, plastics and floods, runs on solar power and stores data offline.

Why: Outfalls flood in the rainy season.

10%

Affordable

Low enough cost per site to cover many outfalls, including upkeep.

Why: The city budget is already stretched.

Solution options

Three ways to catch a discharge

Option A · selected

Automated sensor stations

Solar IoT stations at high-risk outfalls measure pH, dissolved oxygen, turbidity and temperature continuously and send alerts over 4G. Wireless sensor networks let water be monitored remotely, in real time and with little human effort (Pule et al., 2017).

Real time, day and nightTraceable to one outfallHigher start-up costProbes need regular cleaning

Option B

Resident test kits and an app

Trained residents test river water with simple kits and report results through an app, as in the FreshWater Watch programme, where citizen data complements agency monitoring (Hadj-Hammou et al., 2017).

Cheap to startBuilds community involvementNot continuous; misses night dischargesData quality varies

Option C

More frequent manual sampling

Inspectors visit outfalls more often with portable meters and send samples to a laboratory, the traditional method that wireless monitoring is designed to complement (Adu-Manu et al., 2017).

Accurate, legally acceptedUses existing staffLabour-heavy and costly to scaleStill hours to days behind

Design selection

Why sensor stations won

Each option was scored from 1 to 5 on every criterion and multiplied by the criterion’s weight, giving a total out of 100.

Timely 25%Traceable 20%Reliable 20%Clear for residents 15%Durable 10%Affordable 10%
A · Sensor stationsSelected
85
B · Test kits and appNot selected
56
C · Manual samplingNot selected
55

Figure 1. Weighted decision matrix. Each coloured block is one criterion’s contribution to the total.

Option A is the only option that scores highly on both of the most heavily weighted criteria, timeliness and traceability. Its weaknesses, start-up cost and probe maintenance, are addressed in the Implementation plan and Cost analysis.

The team also kept the strongest idea from each other option: from B, residents can report pollution with a photo in the app; from C, every alert is confirmed by a laboratory sample before a fine.

See the scores behind each total

Traceable5 / 5One station per outfall
Reliable4 / 5Three-reading rule; probes can drift
Clear for residents4 / 5Colour map plus SMS
Durable3 / 5Fouling and floods need care
Affordable3 / 5About ₫13.9 million in listed parts per site; installation and upkeep still to be quoted

title: Solution
html:
← Back to Solution

Home / Solution

Solution

How a WaterWatch station turns a polluted reading into a phone alert, and the prototypes that prove it.

Detailed designInside a stationAlert rulesLive demoPrototypingTesting

Detailed design

From the outfall to a phone in seconds

Sense

Probes read the outflow every 2 seconds.

Check

Three readings in a row outside the limit trigger an alert.

Send

Data travels over 4G and is logged with time and place.

Alert

The dashboard and app turn red; residents get a warning.

Confirm

An inspector samples the outfall; the lab result comes before any fine.

Inside a station

Built for a dirty, flooding outfall

Live 3D model: pick a part to fly to it. It follows the sensor simulator in the next section.

Alert rules

When a station raises the alarm

Limits follow the national surface-water regulation QCVN 08:2023/BTNMT (Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment, 2023). During a two-week set-up, each station also learns its own baseline, so a river that is already polluted still shows sudden changes.

pH6.0–8.5

Outside this range is the lowest quality level, D.

Dissolved oxygen< 4 mg/L

Below the minimum for level C water.

Turbidity+50%

QCVN has no turbidity limit, so a sudden rise above baseline signals suspended solids.

TemperatureLogged

Used to correct pH and oxygen readings.

Try the rules

Sensor simulator

Drag a probe value or run a discharge. The cards above, the 3D station and the phone demo all follow this one simulated station.

Simulated station NH-04, Nhuệ River, with a reading every 2 seconds. Use the Report rule for internal pilot alerts after establishing a baseline at the field site. The Team rule remains a simulator comparison. The first station does not require a TDS probe.

Full-screen demo ⤢

Prototyping

Three prototypes, one working chain

Without real sensors, the team split the system into a prototype that works like the station, one that feels like the app and one that looks like the hardware.

What and why

Shows that a station can detect a discharge and raise an alert on its own.

How it was made

An ESP32 circuit on Wokwi, an online simulator. Sliders stand in for the pH, oxygen and turbidity probes; code is in C++.

Form and function

Reads every two seconds, applies the QCVN limits and three-reading rule, publishes readings over MQTT and sends a Telegram alert.

How it was tested

Four scenarios, ten runs each, fed with recorded Hanoi monitoring values.

Results

Detection rate, false alarms, alert time

Changes in version 2

Add after testing

Link the Wokwi circuitEmbed the demo video
What and why

Shows residents and authorities what the readings mean for them.

How it was made

A mobile web app in HTML and JavaScript, fed live by P1 over MQTT and hosted on GitHub Pages. It switches between Vietnamese and English and has a large-text mode.

Form and function

Colour-coded outfall map, alert with plain advice, photo reporting and an authority dashboard.

How it was tested

Five to eight users, including older residents, completed three tasks and a SUS questionnaire.

Results

SUS score, task success, quotes

Add after testing

How it was made

A 3D model in Tinkercad, placed into a photo of a Hanoi embankment.

Form and function

Control box above the flood line, probe cage on an arm, locked frame.

How it was tested

Five people were asked what it does and what worries them.

Results

Feedback summary

Feedback and changes

Feedback from the prototyping forum, user tests and the tutor, and what the team changed.

Add feedback → change list

Limitation

The simulator tests the detection and alert logic, not sensor accuracy in real water. Oxygen probes need frequent calibration, and real outfalls bring fouling and floods, so a field pilot is recommended.

title: Implementation
html:
Home / Implementation

Implementation

Up to three stations in a 36-month pilot, starting when the first station enters service. Add two stations after the first passes acceptance.

1 · Rollout plan2 · Operation3 · Cost analysis4 · Risks and community reaction5 · Life cycle6 · Journey map7 · Recommendations

1 · Rollout plan

Prove one station, then add two

Before launch

Survey and quote

  • Survey proposed sites on the Tô Lịch near Cầu Mới, Cầu Dậu and Cầu Thanh Liệt.
  • Use the estimated first-stage setup allowance of ₫37,023,247; revise against actual purchasing conditions.
  • Agree site access and alert steps.
Station 1

Install and test

  • Run a two-week baseline.
  • Check readings against reference instruments.
  • Measure power use and 4G recovery.
Stations 2 and 3

Expand if it passes

  • Add two stations after acceptance and budget approval; second-stage setup allowance ₫54,637,181.
  • Reuse the tested design and alert steps.
To year 3

Operate and decide

  • Measure detection time, false alarms and app use.
  • Review wear at project close and record each station’s age.
  • Decide on wider rollout from the results.

Gate before buying stations 2 and 3Pass levels are agreed before testing starts.

  • Reference readings meet the agreed tolerances
  • 4G recovery and delivery meet the test targets
  • Measured power supports the planned autonomy
  • An internal test alert reaches the operator
  • Site access, staffing and revised quotes approved

2 · Operation

Who runs it and keeps it working

Proposed roles. Each one still needs a written agreement.

Department of Agriculture and Environment

Owns the stations and data, receives alerts and sends inspectors.

System operator

Runs the platform and repairs stations. Confirm a primary operator and a backup with site access before expanding.

Accredited laboratory

Tests the confirmation sample that supports any fine.

Wards and residents

Share alerts locally, report pollution with photos and help watch the sites.

Three-year service baseline

  1. 6month
  2. 12month
  3. 18month
  4. 24month
  5. 30month
  6. 36+ wear review
6

testing rounds in the shared project period. Included in monthly service routes, with a calibration check and test alert.

16

station checks in the 0/6/6 illustration. The simultaneous-start comparison has 18; recalculate from actual commissioning dates.

48 h

repair target from the time a fault is received. Not yet a signed service agreement.

The budget pays 36 monthly shared field routes, including 96 pH tasks and monthly DO cleaning. Six testing rounds and 16 station checks are included. Early two-monthly DO/turbidity calibration gives 48 tasks each, within the 90-day interval (DFRobot, n.d.-c, n.d.-d, 2026). At project close, station ages are 36/30/30 months; inspect wear and replace only when needed.

3 · Cost analysis

Staged costs and affordability

Basis and scope

Capital expenditure (CAPEX) covers equipment and setup; operating expenditure (OPEX) covers services while active. Q190 core equipment is 13,933,146 VND per station, or 43,482,944 VND for three stations and one optional shared pH kit. These hardware subtotals exclude the remaining pilot costs. The budget uses a historical 25,940 VND/USD assumption, not a current transaction rate (DFRobot, n.d.-a, n.d.-c; Hshop, n.d.-c; LILYGO, n.d.; NDH, n.d.).

The 36-month project starts one station before two more at illustrative month six. The 100W/40Ah power configuration and unquoted items are planning assumptions. Listed prices, market benchmarks and internal allowances are distinguished in Appendix E; simulated results do not establish field performance.

Station 1₫13,933,146

Core equipment

Next two stations₫27,866,292

Core equipment

One shared pH kit₫1,683,506

Included planning reserve

Three stations + kit₫43,482,944

Partial hardware subtotal

Three-year budget

Table 4 estimates 339,314,885 VND including 20% contingency. Its low–high scenarios reflect different allowances, not guaranteed prices. Labour uses 600,000 VND per person-day, informed by published electrical-work benchmarks. Future prices are held constant for comparison (FDI Care, n.d.; Viễn Thông Tia Sáng, n.d.).

Thirty-six monthly field rounds include pH calibration, DO cleaning and the six testing rounds; 16 station checks are not extra journeys. Early DO/turbidity calibration every two months stays within 90 days. Shared hosting is counted once. Renewal, incidents, delivery, supply-tax uncertainty and disposal have separate allowances; full-probe DO reserves cover unavailable cap pricing (DFRobot, n.d.-c, n.d.-d, 2026; Render, n.d.-b).

Table 4. Modelled pilot budget (VND); estimates, not supplier quotations
CategoryThree-year VNDScope
CAPEX91,660,428Equipment, setup and supply reserve
OPEX143,606,000Staff, field routes, services and consumables
Lifecycle47,495,976Parts reserves and collection
Subtotal282,762,404Before general contingency
Contingency (20%)56,552,481Analyst reserve
Three-year planning budget339,314,885Estimate; not a quotation
Low–high scenario260,250,806–468,154,608Alternative assumptions; not a price ceiling

Three-year planning budget: ₫339,314,885

Affordability and payment proposal

A proposed municipal or institutional pilot fund would cover setup. Operations and renewal average about 5.31 million VND per project-month before contingency. This proposal charges households no monitoring fee and assumes no grant, income or unpaid labour. These are proposed funding roles, not commitments; income evidence does not establish affordability. If recurring funding is insufficient, retain one pilot and defer expansion.

Ordering the next two stations requires acceptance and an updated budget. Field power, coverage and repair capacity remain untested; the 48-hour response target is not a contracted service. Contingency does not guarantee performance or unlimited incident coverage.

Supporting records

Appendix E: budget, sources and assumptions · Cost section and appendices (Word)

4 · Risks and community reaction

What could go wrong, and the response

PossibleHigh impact
Readings near the limit are wrong

Listed error is about ±50 NTU for turbidity and ±0.6 mg/L for oxygen (DFRobot, n.d.-b, n.d.-c). Test against reference instruments before buying more.

LikelyMedium impact
Probe fouling and drift

Wiper brush, scheduled cleaning and an extra visit when readings drift.

PossibleHigh impact
Alert fatigue

Test the three-reading rule against the site baseline. Verify readings near the limit with a reference instrument.

PossibleMedium impact
Theft or flooding

Locked cage above the flood line, with ward staff watching the site.

PossibleHigh impact
Factory pushback

Laboratory confirmation before any fine; clusters can use alerts to fix their own treatment.

PossibleMedium impact
Digital divide

SMS and loudspeaker alerts, large text and Vietnamese labels.

5 · Life cycle

A water sensor should not become water pollution

Stage 6 of 6

End of life

Impact
Retired boards become e-waste; AGM batteries need suitable lead-acid collection.
Stakeholders
Certified recycler, the Department
Our response
Review wear in month 36, replace parts only as needed, recycle boards and batteries and reuse cages.

6 · Journey map

What a working station changes

An illustrative scenario: Mrs Lan, 58, farms fish downstream on the Nhuệ in Thanh Trì.

02:00Discharge

Untreated water enters the river upstream of her ponds.

02:01Detected

A station sees oxygen fall for three readings in a row.

02:02Warned

She receives an SMS: do not pump river water tonight.

06:00Protected

She keeps the pond gates shut and her fish survive.

Day 2Followed up

An inspector’s sample goes to the laboratory to confirm the source.

7 · Recommendations

What should happen next

Confirm quotes, operator and payer

Fix the final parts list and who runs and pays for it before ordering; budgeted allowances do not establish funding commitments.

Prove one station in the field

Test accuracy, fouling and battery life at one outfall before buying more.

Agree the legal role of the data

Work with the city on how alerts and laboratory results are used as evidence.

Test with older residents

Check SMS and loudspeaker alerts with people least likely to use the app.

Add ammonium sensing

Ammonium points directly to sewage, which the current probes show only indirectly.

Share and link the data

Publish quality-labelled data and combine it with the city’s river stations.

title: Appendices
html:
Home / Appendices

Appendices

Evidence behind the report. Appendices do not count toward the 4,000-word limit.

Appendix A · Group charter

The team’s agreed roles, meeting times and rules, signed in Week 2.

Link the signed charter

Appendix B · Meeting minutes and decision-matrix session

Weekly minutes: who did what, what was finished and new deadlines, including the session where all members scored the decision matrix.

Link minutes folder

Appendix C · Survey and interviews

Survey questions, anonymised raw responses and interview notes. Participants were told the purpose and no names or phone numbers were collected.

Link raw data

Appendix D · Prototype test data

Scenario results for the sensor station, usability-test task results and SUS scores, and screen recordings.

Link test sheets and videos

Appendix E · Cost model, bill of materials and evidence

Listed prices and internal allowances are separated below. The model includes 36 monthly field routes; its 48 early DO/turbidity calibration tasks supersede the independent historical 32-task calendar for this scenario. No actual funding or field acceptance is claimed.

Appendix E — cost ledger and assumptions

This cost-only appendix separates listings from analyst allowances, not supplier quotations or field results. The independent 32-task strict-90-day illustration is historical; this model uses 48 early two-monthly DO/turbidity tasks within 36 monthly field routes. Six testing rounds and 16 station checks are included in those visits. Hardware renewal figures are funding reserves, not failure predictions (DFRobot, n.d.-c, n.d.-d, 2026; FDI Care, n.d.; Lalamove Vietnam, 2024; Render, n.d.-a; Viễn Thông Tia Sáng, n.d.; Việt Nam Tái Chế, n.d.).
